extracted.intended_audience: literate general public / readers of The Spectator (early 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, didactic/observational periodical essays on manners, fashion, and morals that mix satire, anecdote, and prescriptive commentary for a general reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective duration determined by succession of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Our notion of Time is produced by reflecting on the succession of ideas in our mind; different beings (or states of mind) may perceive the same duration very differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one keeps only one idea in the mind without variation, time seems to have no distance; fixing thoughts intently on one thing 'lets slip out of his Account a good Part of that Duration, and thinks that Time shorter than it is.' Conversely, a quick and constant succession of ideas lengthens the perceived time. Apply this by employing thoughts on many subjects (pursuits of knowledge) to 'extend Life beyond its natural Dimensions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: True affliction is inward and avoids ceremony
rubrics_metrics.description: True Affliction labours to be invisible, is a Stranger to Ceremony, and bears in its own Nature a Dignity much above the little Circumstances which are affected under the Notion of Decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge the sincerity of grief by visible signs (tears, gestures). 'Weeping without much Sorrow' and 'suffering much Sorrow without shedding Tears' both occur; extreme visible signs often indicate superficial passions. Inform 'shallow Critics' that modest, inward grief is more dignified than ostentatious demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive visible emotion often signals superficial feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: As Laughter does not proceed from profound Joy, so neither does Weeping from profound Sorrow; the Heart distended with Grief stops all the Passages for Tears or Lamentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of outward excess as proof of depth. Deep passions frequently manifest quietly; theatrical displays are suspect. Use this when judging characters or real people—look for steadiness and inward signs rather than performative demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of servants reflects example of superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: Servants 'are what we are, according to the Example of our Superiors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the behaviour or morality of servants, consider the influence and examples set by masters and the household environment. The presence of wit and good sense may be found in all orders; avoid blanket moralizing about social classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curb extravagance when fashion or opinion already leans against it
rubrics_metrics.description: An excessive head-dress (or other extravagant fashion) can be most effectually attacked when the Fashion is against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory or critical efforts to suppress absurd extravagance have best effect when public sentiment or fashion already disfavors the excess; sudden or solitary attempts (like a preacher's denunciation) may have temporary results but the fashion can quickly return. Use social tides strategically when advocating for restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain natural proportion and avoid supernumerary ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to add anything ornamental to what is already the masterpiece of Nature; when we load the head with supernumerary ornaments we destroy the symmetry of the human figure and call off the eye from great and real Beauties to childish gewgaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fashion and decoration (and by extension in composition and taste), prefer proportion and restraint. Avoid whimsical superstructures that obscure natural beauty or the main subject; prioritize harmony and the original design of nature/art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punitive deterrence as a legal remedy for honour-based violence (Pharamond's edict)
rubrics_metrics.description: No person who either sends or accepts a challenge, or the posterity of either, shall be capable of bearing office; send/receive a challenge yields personal estate to the other party and vests real estate in the next heir; in appeals for blood, offender suffers death and forfeiture; monarchy cannot pardon these offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of a strict legal regime designed to eradicate duelling by removing social rewards and imposing harsh civil and criminal penalties. As a policy rubric: deter honour-based private violence by removing honour/status benefits, imposing property forfeitures, and denying pardon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer instruction suited to proper sphere and practical duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement of understandings may or may not be of service to women, 'according as it is managed.' It may be better that women improve 'in our own Sphere, and approved our selves better Daughters, Wives, Mothers, and Friends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending education or reading, consider practical applicability to one's social/household roles. Advocate for teaching (e.g., arithmetic, philosophy to subdue passions) that serves real duties rather than mere display of scholarship; urge caution in adopting models meant for different social ranks.
